'''Paolo Giudici''' is an academic and an author. He is a full professor of [[Statistics]] at the [[University of Pavia]]. 

Giudici's research interests include [[statistical inference]] and [[machine learning]], with a particular focus on [[Risk analysis (business)|risk analysis]], [[Explainable artificial intelligence|explainable AI]], and [[Financial technology|financial technologies]].

==Education==
Giudici completed his [[Master of Science]] in [[Economics]] at [[Bocconi University]] in 1989 and his Master of Science in [[Statistics]] at the [[University of Minnesota]] in 1990. Later, he earned his [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in Statistics from the [[University of Trento]] in 1994.<ref name=Cv>{{Cite web|url=https://unipv.academia.edu/paologiudici/CurriculumVitae|title=Paolo Giudici - Curriculum Vitae|website=University of Pavia – Academia.edu|access-date=8 August 2025}}</ref>

==Career==
Giudici began his career as an assistant professor of Statistics at the University of Pavia from 1994 to 1999. At the same institution, he also held other appointments, including associate professor of Statistics at the faculty of Economics from 2000 to 2006, full professor of Statistics at the faculty of Political Sciences from 2007 to 2011, and, since 2012, he has been a full professor of Statistics at the Department of Economics and Management.<ref name=Cv/> 

Giudici has coordinated European-funded research projects, including FIN-TECH and PERISCOPE.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://fbf.eui.eu/people/paolo-giudici/|title=Paolo Giudici|website=EUI – Florence School of Regulation|access-date=August 13, 2025}}</ref> He holds the appointment of specialty chief editor at the ''Artificial Intelligence in Finance (Frontiers)''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/artificial-intelligence/editors|title=Editors – Artificial Intelligence in Finance|website=Frontiers|access-date=13 August 2025}}</ref>

==Research==
To characterize the [[Financial contagion|contagion]] impact between asset prices, Giudici introduced an extended [[Vector autoregression|Vector Autoregressive]] model based on network models, concluding that [[Bitcoin]] prices have a low correlation with traditional assets.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Katsiampa |first1=Paraskevi |last2=Corbet |first2=Shaen |last3=Lucey |first3=Brian |title=High frequency volatility co-movements in cryptocurrency markets |journal=Journal of International Financial Markets, Institutions and Money |date=2019 |volume=62 |pages=35–52 |doi=10.1016/j.intfin.2019.05.003 |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S104244311930023X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Together with Bussmann and others, he proposed an explainable AI model to analyze [[credit management]] and risk during [[peer-to-peer lending]], assessing [[Shapley value]]s, and analyzing 15,000 firms to identify non-risky and risky borrowers, as well as underscoring their financial characteristics.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=David |first1=Mhlanga |title=Financial Inclusion in Emerging Economies: The Application of Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence in Credit Risk Assessment |journal=International Journal of Financial Studies |date=2021 |volume=9 |issue=3 |pages=39 |doi=10.3390/ijfs9030039 |doi-access=free |language=en |hdl=10419/257784 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> He also conducted a study to evaluate two explainable AI models: Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) and SHapley Additive Explanations (SHAP), employing [[XGBoost]] to predict the default probability for [[Small and Medium Enterprises]]. The study highlighted that LIME has less discriminatory power than SHAP.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=Yujia |last2=Calabrese |first2=Raffaella |last3=Martin-Barragan |first3=Belen |title=Interpretable machine learning for imbalanced credit scoring datasets |journal=European Journal of Operational Research |date=2024 |volume=312 |issue=1 |pages=357–372 |doi=10.1016/j.ejor.2023.06.036 |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0377221723005088 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Giudici authored a book titled ''Applied Data Mining: Statistical Methods for Business and Industry'', in which he described applied [[data mining]] techniques (including computational and [[statistical modelling]]) within a unified statistical framework and demonstrated their practical applications.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://search.worldcat.org/title/54350532|title=Applied data mining: statistical methods for business and industry|website=WorldCat|access-date=August 8, 2025}}</ref> Wei Jiang, in his review of the book, stated that "the book provides a detailed presentation of these case studies". However, he described the discussed criterion as "quite brief but transparent" and suggested that "it would be better to provide a clear link between different criteria".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Giudici |first1=Paolo |last2=Jiang |first2=Wei |title=A Review of: "Applied Data Mining – Statistical Methods for Business and Industry" |journal=IIE Transactions |date=2006 |volume=38 |issue=12 |pages=1131 |doi=10.1080/07408170600582880 |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/07408170600582880|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Lesley F. Wright from [[Liverpool John Moores University]] commented that "the book's strength lies in the number and diversity of these case studies".<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wright |first=Lesley F. |date=September 2004 |title=Review of Applied Data Mining: Statistical Methods for Business and Industry |journal=Wiley-Blackwell}}</ref> Richard J. Cleary characterized it as a book with many "nice features". However, he highlighted the presence of "some sections that are perhaps too difficult".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cleary |first1=Richard J. |title=Review of Applied Data Mining: Statistical Methods for Business and Industry |journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association |date=2006 |volume=101 |issue=475 |pages=1317–1318 |doi=10.1198/jasa.2006.s135 |jstor=27590820 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/27590820|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Furthermore, Giudici and Raffinetti expanded the use of Lorenz Zonoids to develop assessment tools for the four main artificial intelligence trustworthiness criteria: S.A.F.E. ([[Sustainability]], [[Accuracy]], [[Fairness (machine learning)|Fairness]], and Explainability).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Černevičienė |first1=Jurgita |last2=Kabašinskas |first2=Audrius |title=Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in finance: a systematic literature review |journal=Artificial Intelligence Review |date=2024 |volume=57 |issue=8 |pages=216 |doi=10.1007/s10462-024-10854-8 |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-024-10854-8 |language=en|doi-access=free }}</ref>
